Jacques Ellul <1>(1968)</1> describes technique as a system that ceases to operate as a mere instrument and comes to present itself as a reality of its own, no longer limited to being a means, but capable of imposing its logic as an object in itself <2>Ellul</2><3>(Ellul, 1968, p. 65)</3>.

This dynamic is driven by efficiency and tends to select the most effective method automatically, so that, once the efficiency criterion is measured and established, technique consolidates and expands by its own force <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 82-83)</2>.
Technique reaches a point at which it comes to transform itself and progress with little decisive intervention by man <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 88-89)</2>.

For this reason, its effects go beyond the productive level and take on a civilizational dimension, insofar as technique expands into all domains, tends to reduce man to the condition of an object and imposes itself as the substance of the social world, and can be described as an entire civilization <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 5; p. 128)</2>.

In this scenario, values and ends lose centrality because technical rationality operates as a machine of instrumentalization, converting everything into means and shifting the decision criterion to the performance of the method and to what works best <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 145)</2>.
Ellul <1>(1968)</1> insists that the technical phenomenon cannot be treated as a particular sector of modernity, because it tends to cut across the very elements of civilization.

The decisive point is that, in any domain where it is applied, technique presents itself as a rational process, which shifts the social problem into a problem of method <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 81)</2>.

Ellul <1>(1968)</1> links the obsession with efficiency and productivity to the production of an inhuman atmosphere, in which work is dehumanized and man moves away from nature <2>Ellul</2><3>(Ellul, 1968, p. 3)</3>.

At the political-economic level, he argues that technique favors the formation of an aristocracy of technicians, capable of concentrating knowledge and decisions in opaque circuits barely accessible to the lay public <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 165)</2>.

When this framework is joined to the State, democracy is weakened because public debate tends to be replaced by management and mechanisms of persuasion, with corrosive effects on the citizen's capacity for discernment <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 281)</2>.

For Jacques Ellul <1>(1968)</1>, “technique” is not equivalent to machines, nor to the mechanical apparatus taken in isolation: “Whoever says technique immediately thinks of machine”, but this identification is a recurring error <2>Ellul</2><3>(Ellul, 1968, p. 1)</3>.

This is because technique “has now assumed almost complete autonomy in relation to the machine”, going beyond the status of a mere instrument and coming to operate as a phenomenon of its own <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 2)</2>.

Seen this way, technique presents itself as rationalization driven by efficiency, insofar as the “satisfactory” and “efficient” method tends to impose itself on its own — the “one best way” mentioned earlier — and, with this, the technical decision takes the form of an objective necessity: “there is no choice between two technical methods: one imposes itself fatally because its results are counted, measured, patent and indisputable” <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 83)</2>.

By penetrating “into all domains and into man himself” and tending to involve the maximum of domains in order to be effective, technique ceases to be merely an object for man and “becomes his very substance”, acquiring a totalizing reach <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 5)</2>.

In this generalization, its performance criteria become a practical measure of social decision, and the autonomy of the technical system restricts the possibility of human deliberation about ends: “the autonomy of technique therefore prevents man, at present, from choosing his destiny” <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 143)</2>.

For this reason, the technical phenomenon cannot be reduced to machines or material apparatuses, since it includes organizational factors and utilitarian modes of thought that structure social life <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 1-5)</2>.

In this framework, technique presents itself as indifferent to moral judgments and breaks with the belief that technical progress would be equivalent, by itself, to human progress <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 117)</2>.

The distinction between ancient and modern technique makes this shift explicit: while the former remains tied to empiricism and slow development, the latter is characterized by universality, objective rationality, artificiality, automatism, self-augmentation, indivisibility and autonomy, with effects capable of reaching all aspects of human life, including the reduction of man to the condition of an object <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 66-80)</2>.

It is in this context that Ellul describes the automatism of technical choice as a blind search for the “best way” of performing a task, with the loss of a holistic criterion of adequacy and growing indifference to the social, moral or aesthetic consequences produced by the method <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 82-88)</2>.

On the plane of artificiality, Ellul states that modern technique opposes nature and constitutes a system made up of artificial means, in which technical intervention reduces the real to a “logical scheme” and reorganizes facts and phenomena according to internal demands of rationalization <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 82)</2>.

This environment breaks with the traditional anchor, since technique rejects tradition and comes to rely on the combination and accelerated evolution of earlier technical processes, at a pace too fast for full integration into the accumulated cultural fabric <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 13)</2>.

The economy, in this framework, becomes progressively dependent on technique and its methods, to the point where technique ceases to function as a subordinate economic instrument and comes to dictate the conditions of the economic game itself <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 152-162)</2>.

Ellul characterizes technique as a fundamental instrument of state power, especially in the modern State, increasingly dependent on technical procedures to administer, regulate, control and wage war <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 233-238)</2>.

This dependence shapes the state structure, favors centralization and bureaucratization and alters the very nature of the State, which comes to operate as a technical organism, limited by the forms of perception and decision that its administrative rationality makes available <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 257-260)</2>.

Examining techniques aimed directly at man, designed to modify behavior, needs and subjective dispositions, Ellul identifies psychological, sociological and biometric techniques as telling manifestations of attempts to control and manipulate the human person <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 325-331)</2>.

The author also observes that the technical modification of space itself can condition behavior, which extends the problem beyond isolated instruments and reaches the environmental organization of human action <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 331-335)</2>.

At the end of his work, Ellul questions the belief in technical progress as an objective synonym for human progress and appeals to individual and collective responsibility in the face of technique <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 441-445)</2>.

Taken together, this makes it possible to identify the point of passage to the legal problem: by reducing the real to a “logical scheme” and refusing external judgments when the problem is presented as technical, technique compresses the space for deliberation about ends and shifts the decision into the language of efficiency <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 82; p. 136)</2>.

On the plane of operative rationality, the shift appears when, to escape “arbitrariness and subjectivity” and “ethical judgment”, technique requires reality to be reduced to number <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 17)</2>.

For the “technician of law”, the decisive reference tends to stop being the normative end and to become efficiency of application, since “all law depends on its efficiency” and “a law that is not applied is not a law” <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 299)</2>.

Under this pressure for performance and operability, normative conflicts tend to be reconfigured as problems of management and compliance, making it harder to deliberate about ends when technical autonomy narrows the space of choice about collective means and directions <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 143)</2>.

Ellul <1>(1968)</1> describes technique as a process that tends to impose itself in practice with the force of necessity, not because it is “good” or “bad”, but because, once available, it comes to be used.

The author formulates this directly by stating that “everything that is technical, without distinction of good and evil, is necessarily used when it is at our disposal”, which shifts public debate from the field of moral choice to the field of inevitable adoption <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 102-103)</2>.

Discussing cinema, for example, Ellul observes that censorship can limit themes, but does not touch “the essential”, which is the “psychic modification of man” caused by the “violent impression of the film”; the inevitable emotion “modifies the psychological tone” and tends to make man “the component of a crowd” <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 291)</2>.

Ellul <1>(1968, p. 82-85)</1> describes modern technique as methodical and systematic, characteristics that also shape the dynamics of the entertainment industry as it exploits technologies to maximize its reach and engagement.

For Postman <1>(2006)</1> and Ellul <2>(1968)</2>, technique imposes rationalities, rhythms and criteria of relevance that reorder social experience and make certain consequences predictable without their being presented as explicit normative decisions.

From a Brazilian standpoint, Ladislau Dowbor <1>(2025)</1> stands out for his critique of what he calls “rentier capitalism”, a transformative system that is said to have redesigned global dynamics and marked a significant break from earlier modes of production.

“The result is so-called ‘demand monopolies’: we have to use what others use, because without it we cannot communicate, not to mention that they buy up any competitor that tries to make room for itself” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24)</2>.

The core of command thus shifts from the domain of manufacture to the capture of the process, since whoever controls the platform controls the points of entry and permanence and can turn each crossing into a toll <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 13; p. 20; p. 51-52)</2>.
Rentiers earn not so much from the services they provide as from everyone's obligation to pass through their turnstiles.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21)</2>.

In the informational environment, the toll economy is realized with special effectiveness through legal-technical enclosures, since intellectual property rights, license contracts, account architecture and access control mechanisms become governance infrastructure and turn access to and permanence in the ecosystem into a recurring source of extraction <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 7; p. 21; p. 41)</2>.

Inserted in ecosystems of signs whose permanence is conditioned by contractual and technological turnstiles, the consumer is induced by anticipation and by promises of availability, continuity and functionality that they cannot reconstruct in their decisive elements, since delivery does not come with transparency criteria about its limitations and, in practice, can be fully and unilaterally modulated by the supplier <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 19-21)</2>.

In this scenario, the very justification of intellectual property tends to operate in an instrumental key, tied to the incentive for future creations <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</2>, so that the hypertrophy of duration and scope may produce a mismatch between incentive and blockage.

In copyright, profits tend to be concentrated in the first cycles of exploitation, around five or, at most, ten years after publication, while exclusivity may last for decades, becoming a fence that restricts access <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2>.
For this reason, Dowbor <1>(2024, p. 13)</1> argues that rentierism appropriates the surplus without a corresponding productive contribution.

The disproportion between effective productive contribution and observed enrichment no longer indicates a peripheral distortion and instead points to a qualitative shift in the systemic dynamic, in which the rentier logic becomes the organizing principle <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8-9; p. 20)</2>.
Along these lines, profit on production evolved into rentierism on intermediation <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 68)</2>.

By consolidating computing, logistics and intermediation services and circuits on which third parties come to depend in order to operate, an infrastructure rentierism is formed, sustained by recurring tolls and by structurally unreplicable barriers to entry, anchored in scale, integration and systemic dependence <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>.

Value extraction stabilizes through position and control of points of passage, such as networks, infrastructures and intermediations, and not through a correlated increase in social utility, reorganizing accumulation as a systematic drain of social wealth <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 13; p. 20)</2>.

In the informational paradigm, knowledge takes the position of central factor of production, but its economic logic is not the same as that of physical goods, since, unlike material goods, shared knowledge is not lost to whoever shares it, as it is not a rival good and access to it can be generalized <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 11)</2>.

The decisive point for the present analysis is not to deny the persistence of the productive base, but to show its structural subordination to informational-financial command, which comes to define who accesses the market, through which mediations and under which conditions of subjection <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 27)</2>.

Along these lines, the author states that billions of people cease to represent an incalculable mass and become isolable individuals, sources of information and customers, whether they like it or not <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</2>.

In this horizon, the offer ceases to operate as a uniform, previously knowable standard and comes to function as a contingent set of conditions modulated by continuous segmentation and optimization <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28)</2>.

It is this tension between emancipatory potential and rentier appropriation that makes the ontological transition described by Dowbor at once a critique of the present and a dispute over the institutional destiny of the digital <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 10-11; p. 42; p. 45)</2>.

This diagnosis is condensed in the description of everyday life mediated by platforms and payment systems, which leads the author to conclude that a system of micro-drainage of resources and personal information of billions of people has been generated <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</2>.

Dowbor <1>(2024)</1> presents digital rentierism as the central economic vector of the 21st century and identifies, at the top of this machinery, platform conglomerates that occupy a dominant position in the organization of markets, in informational circulation and in demand itself.

Addressing the theme, Dowbor shifts the focus from individual luxury to the dynamics of reinvestment and expansion of capacities, stating that the point is not to have yachts and planes, but to have a company generating profits that will be reinvested in more productive capacity <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 5)</2>.

At the distributive level, the shift is expressed in the rupture between appropriation of the surplus and productive contribution and in the drain of social wealth typical of unproductive rentierism, breaking the minimum of proportionality between how much one contributes and how much one gains <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 13; p. 20)</2>.

“A very important dimension is the basic logic of information systems financed by advertising: the return depends on maximizing engagement, attention, which leads the media in general, and social media in particular, to favor the news that attracts the most” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 30-31)</2>.

The same rationality that organizes the individual experience of consumption also reconfigures the public sphere under a structurally interested bias; for this reason, the “maximization of profit and dividends sits poorly with the dissemination of science and culture” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 30- 31)</2>.

The diagnosis appears when the author describes the battle for people's attention time in the context of the predominance of the communication and information industry <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 25)</2> and, even more incisively, when he states that, caught in the web of the system, we pay at every step, both in costs and in the time of our attention <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</4>.

A capture that weighs, in the words of the author, who describes it as a subjective imprisonment inherent to this regime, “on our pockets” and “on our minds” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 30)</2>.
That is, the “information that platforms capture is free”, while “private information is appropriated for free” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 66)</2>.
The result is so-called demand monopolies, in which it becomes necessary to use what others use, on pain of functional isolation <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24)</2>.

The resulting compulsoriness combines with strategies of neutralizing competitors by acquisition and incorporation, reinforcing the concentration and planetary expansion of the dominant agent <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24; p. 31)</2>.

For the author, this is not competition to provide better services at better prices, since these structures charge what they want, from people and companies across the whole planet <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>.

The replacement of WordPerfect by Word, when a specific standard became dominant, illustrates the conversion of voluntary adherence into operational necessity and, with it, the feasibility of arbitrary charging on a global scale, with macroeconomic effects the author connects to inflation driven by monopoly profits (profit-inflation) <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>.

The axis of accumulation ceases to gravitate around profit derived from material production and shifts to the capture of flows (of payment, of data, of decisions and of visibility) converted into value by the continuous measurement and modulation of circulation and behavior in a governed environment <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-31)</2>.

It operates as a device by which value extraction is converted into social control and subordinates even traditional companies to the logic of value for the shareholder, that is, to shareholder value <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 27-28)</2>.

The mechanisms of extraction become progressively more complex and, for this reason, less understood <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3)</2>, causing financial-digital exploitation to remain “a nebulous reality” for almost the entire population <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 13)</4>.

Dowbor makes explicit the gap between a digital economic base and still analog institutions by stating that the economic base has shifted and the institutions remain in the last century <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8)</2>.
He also observes that immaterial money allows sophisticated forms of exploitation that are hard to understand <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 84)</2>.
The synthesis appears when he states that it is always a matter of transforming threatening abundance into a new form of scarcity <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 22)</2>.

The change is profound because it marks the passage from an era of producers and buyers to an era of providers and users <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</2>, in which the central economic mechanism ceases to be the good and becomes the process.
In this sense, today one is the owner of a process and charges for its use <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 52)</2>.

Because of this, enjoyment is sustained by continuous technical-operational support and, consequently, unilateral changes in parameters of availability, compatibility or maintenance can degrade, reconfigure or extinguish the functional value delivered to the consumer, without this being reduced to mere contractual variation, since they bear directly on the practical conditions of delivery that make the experience possible over time <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40; p. 51-52)</2>.

In Dowbor's diagnosis, this governance rests on the supplier's infrastructural dominance, which concentrates “control of the access codes” and “the management of content” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40)</2>.

The theoretically central form of “continuous change” is that, in consumption based on repeated access, the conditions of use cease to be fixed and are instead renewed, modulated and charged recurrently <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

Thus, when the economic object shifts from “good” to “process”, access becomes structurally conditional and revisable, administered as a continuous permission, which makes the unilateral reconfiguration of the rules of enjoyment possible <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

In this regime, the monetization of the immaterial depends on an institutional engineering that converts technically cheap circulation into conditioned access, fabricating scarcity and ensuring that knowledge is only realized as price when its diffusion is contained <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 22; p. 41; p. 51-52)</2>.

In immaterial objects of consumption, utility is not exhausted in the act of acquisition, since it depends on continuous decisions of support, updating and continuity under the supplier's control <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52; p. 57)</2>.

These are calculation procedures oriented to maximizing return and sustained by an algorithmic capillarity that the user cannot reconstruct by ordinary means <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>.

The caveat is decisive to avoid a naturalizing reading of the demand monopoly, showing that the coercion of the technological standard does not result from technical neutrality, but from a technique organized by specific regimes of property, governance and institutional design <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 39-40; p. 45; p. 56; p. 66; p. 88)</2>.
In this register, he observes that the cost of credit is adjusted according to the bank's interests <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</2>.

Informational asymmetry, from Dowbor's perspective, is not only a classical theme of political economy about the relationship between buyer and seller, but a systemic architecture in which platforms and intermediaries accumulate hypertrophic capacities to see and calculate, while users and the State itself remain in a state of cognitive blindness <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>.
And it was legalized” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</2>.

This asymmetry becomes power of command because it enables discriminatory pricing, understood as individualized modulation of the price and conditions of the same service — and, in digital ecosystems, also of the conditions of access to and enjoyment of IOCs — based on inferences about profile, urgency and propensity to pay, operated by proprietary criteria and without comparable transparency <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>.

By citing Stiglitz as a reference for understanding these impacts, Dowbor places the diagnosis within a consolidated tradition on informational asymmetry and inequality <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 48)</2>: in the digital environment, the ordinary capture of data from connected life radically amplifies this asymmetry and makes it structural, guiding economic decisions directed against individuals themselves.

First, in the explanation that, in the economy of the immaterial, under rentier logic, business strategy tends to maximize the locking of access to produce monopoly effects <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 22-23)</2>.

Second, in the formulation that knowledge only acquires sale value when its diffusion is prevented by legal and repressive apparatuses, producing artificial scarcity linked to the idea of a “toll” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 41)</2>.
Third, in the generalization of “toll capitalism”, in which access to processes and environments is fenced in to sustain permanent rent <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

Finally, at the infrastructural level, when discussing the capacity of private operators to dictate who accesses the infoways through “communication corrals” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 49-50)</2>, that is, forms of closure that convert circulation into passage conditioned and administrable by a proprietary ecosystem.

In “Os desafios da revolução digital: libertar conhecimento para o bem comum”, Dowbor <1>(2024)</1> deepens this passage from industrial capitalism to a configuration dominated by digital rentierism, in which accumulation shifts from production to the extraction of rent through control of intangible assets and intermediation infrastructures.

Dowbor grounds “demand monopolies” in the specificity of the immaterial, which circulates on a planetary scale and with low territoriality, favoring accelerated concentrations: “the worlds of money, knowledge and communication [...] are, precisely, immaterial [...] they circulate [...] in planetary space, without the old ‘territoriality’” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24)</2>.

On this basis, the network effect converts standard into coercion: the utility of the system depends on others' adherence, making the choice functionally compulsory; moreover, expansion is reinforced by neutralizing competitors through acquisition or incorporation <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24)</2>.

Dowbor condenses the transition to rentierism in the rupture between appropriation of the surplus and productive contribution, setting the criterion of proportionality: when “a minimum of proportionality between how much people contribute productively, and how much they grow rich” is broken, the system ceases to operate as accumulation and comes to function as “unproductive rentierism”, that is, a “drain of social wealth” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 20)</2>.

In dialogue with contemporary typologies, Dowbor mobilizes Brett Christophers to group the main varieties of rentierism into seven sources: Financial, Natural resource reserves, Intellectual property, Digital platforms, Service contracts, Infrastructure and Land <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 20)</2>.

The distinction between profit and rent in Dowbor serves to locate the change in the axis of accumulation: profit tends to be linked to reinvestment and the expansion of productive capacity, while rent stabilizes as capture by position and intermediation — that is, gain derived from control of a “point of passage” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 5)</2>.

This precision also has a linguistic dimension, since current usage mixes up productive income and toll income, naturalizing the idea of “investment” for unproductive applications <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 20)</2>.

Without eliminating the ambivalence, Dowbor observes that certain services may be useful and, even so, operate with disproportionate extraction typical of intermediation oligopolies, when the gain stems less from productive input than from the inevitability of the crossing <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21)</2>.

The expression “unit treatable by calculation” condenses, in Dowbor, the reconfiguration of the user as an individual isolable and governable by inference, converted simultaneously into a source of information, risk and return, by virtue of algorithmic capillarity and orientation to financial maximization <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>.

In this regime, the offer ceases to operate as a uniform standard and comes to admit continuous modulation (through frictions, permissions, advantages and limits) producing functionally differentiated deliveries under the appearance of an “equal” service, without the consumer being able to reconstitute, by ordinary means, the criteria of the variation <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>.

The specific contribution of “micro-drainage” is not to reiterate that there is fractional extraction, but to make explicit its evidentiary effect: the intermediation chain is only intelligible to whoever holds operational traces (logs, metrics, recommendation or ranking parameters, pricing and modulation criteria), so that the intermediary can reconstruct the link between data capture, profiling and automated decisions, while the user remains confined to the surface of the interface and to the perceived effects <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>.

In Dowbor, behavioral influence stems from the economic design of systems financed by advertising: if revenue depends on maximizing engagement and attention time, curation and recommendation mechanisms tend to favor what retains the user, making informational architecture a direct function of profitability <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 30-31)</2>.

At the dogmatic level, the sensitive point is the opacity of ordering criteria: signs such as “relevance”, “trends” and “personalization” may conceal rankings oriented by engagement metrics and advertising return, straining duties of transparency and loyalty in the governance of the user's informational experience <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 30- 31)</2>.
The material presupposition is individualization at scale: “8 billion people […] become isolable individuals, sources of information” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</2>.

Seen this way, screen time, clicks, searches and browsing trajectories cease to be neutral residues and come to compose a diffuse production of behavioral signals that feeds profiling, segmentation and modulation of conduct, converting experience into raw material for valorization <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29; p. 66)</2>.

At the dogmatic level, the point is not to equate user and employee, but to show that the enjoyment of the IOC takes place in an environment of opaque governance of the collection, processing and economic use of data, which prevents the consumer from auditing the correspondence between signs of “service”, “personalization” and “free of charge” and the real conditions of exploitation, updating factual vulnerability in its semiotic aspect and straining duties of transparency and informational loyalty <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 66)</2>.

In Dowbor, capture oriented by retention and return metrics depends on an architecture that organizes the visible, the desirable and the probable, converting attention and behavior into economic input at an individualizable scale <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29-30)</2>.

The author insists, however, on the ambivalence of the technological base, whose political materialization can either sustain forms of democratic connectivity or expand the capacity for corporate manipulation on a larger scale <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 39)</2>.

Gigantism, far from being a competitive accident, stems from technical characteristics that accelerate concentration and make domination rapidly planetary <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24)</2>, converting standards into coercion.

Dowbor uses the term inflation by monopoly profits (profit-inflation) for the macroeconomic effect of the pricing power exercised by private intermediation infrastructures when dominant standards and points of passage become inevitable, so that rising fees and commissions come to be reflected as inflation without depending on classical demand pressures or cost shocks: “When these prices rise and impact inflation, they generate inflation by monopoly profits (profit-inflation).” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>.
